societies.name: Uglies (Tally’s New Pretty Town before the mind-rain)
societies.society: The supported young New Pretty cohort in Tally’s city

scope.period: The established Prettytime before the mind-rain
scope.population: Living New Pretties, approximately sixteen to twenty-five, in Tally’s New Pretty Town
exclusions: Middle Pretty workforce assigned this leisure pattern
All independent cities treated as one government
Film continuity assigned unverified book institutions

societies.description:
New Pretty Town supplies its young residents with food, housing and entertainment without ordinary wage purchase. Apartment wall systems manufacture many requested goods from raw inputs. This establishes a continuing technologically supported cohort, rather than a single wealthy teenager. The strong guarantee estimate applies within that status-defined group; entry depends on the compulsory operation, and it is not a promise of equal freedom or the same support outside the city.

Control remains concentrated in human city institutions, including the authorities that enforce surgery and suppress resistance. Asking a wall for an item does not give the recipient ownership of its supply. Young New Pretties are mainly described as enjoying parties and recreation, while later Middle Pretties take occupations. That supports a high, broadly uncertain nonworking estimate for the young cohort only. Useful creative activity and exceptional responsibilities still count as work, so the estimate is not a literal statement that everyone does nothing. The later political transformation and its new resource pressures are covered separately.

guarantees.basis: Food, shelter and entertainment are explicitly free within the admitted New Pretty cohort; compulsory status and exclusion qualify universality.

control.basis: Human city authorities enforce the system and retain effective control; resident requests are not productive ownership.

nonworking.basis: Secondary setting accounts put this young cohort in a prolonged recreation phase before later occupations. This is an editorial age-cohort estimate allowing useful chosen activity, not a canonical census.

evidence.claim: New Pretties receive free material support and use wall fabrication while human authorities control their status.
evidence.locator: Series setting and New Pretty Town apartment entries

uncertainties: Only the young supported cohort is counted; the adult workforce remains outside this denominator.
Book and film economics are not merged.
The numerical participation estimate is provisional and secondary.

review.method: Second pass against the gathered passages, including explicit uncertainty; no independent reviewer

societies.name: Extras (Aya’s Japanese reputation economy)
societies.society: The unnamed Japanese city’s post-mind-rain allocation system

scope.period: The functioning reputation economy three years after the mind-rain
scope.population: Living residents of Aya Fuse’s city
exclusions: All Japanese or global cities assigned this system
Future space settlements treated as completed

societies.description:
Aya’s city retains fabrication technology but changes how people obtain its output. Citizens gain access through merits for useful tasks or through reputation, with fame affecting resources and privileges. The resource limits are real: freeing people from the old mental conditioning increases demand. This is a distinct arrangement from the earlier New Pretty cohort, because social visibility now becomes an alternative route to material access. It is not unlimited abundance.

The control estimate is cautiously positive: residents can seek resources through their own actions and changing public attention, yet influential people gain disproportionate leverage over a centralized allocation system. The sources do not establish equal ownership or an independent machine sovereign. They also do not settle whether every obscure resident retains a secure minimum of food, shelter and care, so the guarantee coordinate remains unresolved. Useful projects, journalism and other work continue, whether paid in merits or rewarded with attention. No population-wide nonworking share follows from the reputation mechanism. The regime label is therefore provisional.

guarantees.basis: Rank affects goods and privilege, but the accessible accounts do not settle a universal subsistence floor.

control.basis: Changing public reputation gives residents some effective access power while concentrating leverage among the famous; productive asset ownership remains unverified.

nonworking.basis: Merits explicitly reward useful work, and journalism can be useful work; no resident participation census is given.

evidence.claim: Wall fabrication is coupled to useful-task merits and face-rank allocation after the mind-rain.
evidence.locator: Reputation economy entry; novel introduction and Doctorow review

uncertainties: Regime 4 is provisional: a guaranteed floor could favor regime 2 and more concentrated effective control could favor regime 3.
Reputation inequality is not automatically proof that basic needs are denied.
No post-ending orbital economy or automatic global constitution is inferred.

review.method: Second pass against the gathered passages, including explicit uncertainty; no independent reviewer

decisions.reason: The Toll’s departure and revival plans do not establish one settled Tonist or post-Thunderhead economy.
decisions.analysis: Earth’s later order, starship support and destination settlements are separate periods; they cannot inherit the early Thunderhead guarantees without evidence.
decisions.follow_up: Skip ending reconstruction and preserve the early record’s narrower scope.

decisions.reason: A Cirrus viewpoint is verified, but the short collection review does not establish a completed offworld allocation system.

decisions.follow_up: Skip reading the collection to rescue the lead.

decisions.reason: The Community assigns actual human occupations without verified available automatic replacement.
decisions.analysis: Equality, planning and assigned work are not themselves post-work or deliberate unnecessary employment; book and movie mechanisms remain separate.

decisions.reason: Eejits remain human workers despite implanted control.
decisions.analysis: Neurological coercion does not turn the agricultural workforce into nonhuman automation or erase it from the work count.

decisions.reason: Matt’s succession and emancipation effort do not establish a technologically supported successor economy.
decisions.analysis: Ending coercion changes rights, but it does not by itself replace human agricultural production or establish labor-independent access.
decisions.follow_up: Skip sequel reconstruction; no precise reader-reported ending mechanism is adopted.

decisions.reason: Free cohort provision and wall fabrication establish a distinct supported New Pretty arrangement.
Reputation/merit allocation of fabricated output establishes a different later economic mechanism, with the basic floor unresolved.
Shreve’s dynasty and body-double conflict do not establish its material-support economy.
decisions.analysis: The same universe does not transfer Tally’s earlier guarantees or Aya’s reputation rules into Shreve.

decisions.reason: Shipboard memory control and stasis do not establish a labor-independent active population’s access system.
decisions.analysis: A Collective takeover can organize human work and coercion without replacing material production; dormant passengers are not active leisure citizens.
